cues.text: A Confirming Council
Four years after the Council of Hippo had first formally listed the twenty-seven books of the New Testament, bishops of the African provinces gathered again at Carthage in 397.
They conducted the ordinary business of provincial church governance and reaffirmed the same canon of Scripture their predecessors had settled at Hippo four years earlier.
This gave it the added authority of a second, independently convened council, rather than resting on a single prior ruling alone.
Augustine, Now a Bishop
Where Augustine had attended the Council of Hippo as a newly ordained priest, by 397 he sat among Carthage’s assembled bishops as Bishop of Hippo himself.
Having been consecrated the previous year, he was still a relatively young bishop among the churchmen shaping the settled scriptural canon of the whole African Church.
He would draw upon that body of teaching constantly across the following three decades of preaching and controversy.
Reaffirming the Twenty-Seven Books
Carthage's canon, closely mirroring Hippo's own list, named the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, and the thirteen Pauline epistles.
It also named the Letter to the Hebrews, the seven Catholic epistles, and the Book of Revelation—the identical twenty-seven books constituting the New Testament in Catholic Bibles today.
This was now confirmed by two successive African councils within the space of a single decade.
An African Consensus, Not Yet a Universal Decree
It is worth noting plainly that neither Hippo nor Carthage functioned as an ecumenical council binding the whole universal Church by their own authority alone.
Their significance lies rather in how faithfully and quickly their settled African consensus came to be received and echoed by the wider Latin Church.
This was aided considerably by the towering theological authority Augustine himself would go on to carry for the rest of his career.
It was also aided by the fact that their canon matched, in substance, the list already associated with Pope Damasus's Roman synod of 382.
Legacy
Together, Hippo and Carthage represent the effective closing of the New Testament canon within the Western Church.
Over a thousand years later, the Council of Trent would define this process with full and binding dogmatic authority in response to the Reformation's own disputes over Scripture.
Yet Trent changed its actual content not at all from what these two modest African councils had already settled in the space of a single Christian generation.

Few pairs of regional councils, so lightly remembered outside specialist study, have shaped so completely and so permanently the physical shape of the book every subsequent Christian would call the Bible.
